weeks.babyDevelopment: The fertilized egg is dividing rapidly and traveling to the uterus. The foundations for your baby's entire body are being laid. This tiny cluster of cells already carries all the genetic information that makes your baby uniquely them.
weeks.momBody: You may not feel any different yet. Technically, this week counts from your last menstrual period, so conception may not have happened yet. Your body is preparing for the incredible journey ahead by thickening the uterine lining.
tipsForWeek: Start taking folic acid 400mcg daily if you haven't already
Avoid alcohol, smoking, and recreational drugs
Eat a balanced diet rich in leafy greens, legumes, and whole grains
Schedule a preconception appointment with your healthcare provider
weeks.nutritionTip: Start prenatal vitamins with folic acid to prevent neural tube defects. Folic acid is most critical in the very early weeks of pregnancy.
weeks.exerciseTip: Light walking and gentle stretching are perfect right now. Continue any regular exercise routine you already have.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Ovulation is occurring this week, and fertilization may happen. The sperm and egg unite to form a zygote — a single cell with a complete set of chromosomes that will determine your baby's sex, eye color, hair, and so much more.
weeks.momBody: You may notice mild ovulation symptoms like slight pelvic pain or increased discharge. Your body temperature may rise slightly after ovulation. This is when the magic can happen!
tipsForWeek: Track ovulation signs if trying to conceive
Stay hydrated — aim for 8–10 glasses of water daily
Get plenty of rest and manage stress
Continue taking prenatal vitamins
weeks.nutritionTip: Iron-rich foods like spinach, lentils, and lean red meat are great to incorporate now. Good iron stores support the major blood volume increase ahead.
weeks.exerciseTip: Enjoy moderate-intensity activities. Swimming, cycling, and yoga are all wonderful choices this week.

weeks.babyDevelopment: The zygote has become a blastocyst — a hollow ball of cells that is implanting into the uterine lining. The inner cells will become your baby, while the outer cells will become the placenta. This is implantation week!
weeks.momBody: Implantation can cause light spotting (called implantation bleeding) and mild cramping. Your body begins producing hCG (the pregnancy hormone) which will soon make a home pregnancy test turn positive.
tipsForWeek: Don't panic about light spotting — it can be normal implantation bleeding
Avoid over-the-counter medications without consulting your doctor
Start reducing caffeine intake to under 200mg per day
Get extra sleep — your body is working incredibly hard
weeks.nutritionTip: Calcium is important for your baby's developing bones. Dairy products, fortified plant milks, broccoli, and almonds are excellent sources.
weeks.exerciseTip: Gentle yoga and walking are ideal. Avoid very intense workouts during implantation week. Listen to your body.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is now called an embryo! Three layers of cells are forming: the ectoderm (which becomes the brain and skin), mesoderm (heart, muscles, bones), and endoderm (digestive system, lungs). The neural tube — the foundation of the brain and spinal cord — is beginning to form.
weeks.momBody: A home pregnancy test will now likely be positive. You may notice your period is late. Some women experience tender breasts, mild nausea, fatigue, or increased urination. Your uterus is about the size of a pear.
tipsForWeek: Take a home pregnancy test if your period is late
Call your OB or midwife to schedule your first prenatal appointment
Continue folic acid supplementation — it's critical right now
Avoid raw fish, deli meats, and unpasteurized cheeses
weeks.nutritionTip: Folate (from food) and folic acid (supplement) are both important. Load up on dark leafy greens, avocado, beans, and citrus fruits.
weeks.exerciseTip: Continue your normal exercise routine with modifications. Avoid contact sports and activities with high fall risk.

weeks.babyDevelopment: The heart is beginning to form and will start beating this week — around 100–160 times per minute! The brain, spinal cord, and other organs are starting to develop. Tiny arm and leg buds are just beginning to appear. Your baby is growing incredibly fast.
weeks.momBody: Morning sickness may begin — though it can strike any time of day. Fatigue can be intense as your body ramps up progesterone. Breast tenderness often intensifies. You might notice you need to urinate more frequently.
tipsForWeek: Eat small, frequent meals to manage nausea
Keep crackers by your bedside for morning sickness
Stay hydrated even if you feel queasy
Rest whenever you can — fatigue is completely normal
weeks.nutritionTip: Ginger can help with nausea — try ginger tea, ginger chews, or ginger ale. Vitamin B6 (found in bananas, chickpeas, potatoes) also helps reduce nausea.
weeks.exerciseTip: Even a 10-minute walk can boost your energy and mood. Listen to your body — on hard nausea days, rest is exercise enough.

weeks.babyDevelopment: The heart is now beating and can often be seen on an early ultrasound. Facial features are beginning to form — dark spots mark where the eyes will be, and small indentations show where the ears will develop. The brain is dividing into its different regions and growing rapidly.
weeks.momBody: Morning sickness may be at its most intense. Your uterus has doubled in size. Heightened sense of smell is common and can trigger nausea. You may feel emotional and that's completely okay — hormones are surging.
tipsForWeek: Avoid strong smells that trigger nausea — use unscented products if needed
Eat protein-rich snacks before bed to help with morning sickness
Consider wearing acupressure wristbands for nausea
Talk to your partner about how you're feeling
weeks.nutritionTip: Protein helps stabilize blood sugar and reduces nausea. Try nuts, nut butter, cheese, eggs, or Greek yogurt as snacks throughout the day.
weeks.exerciseTip: Prenatal yoga can be wonderful for both nausea and emotional balance. Even gentle stretching counts as movement.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is now about the size of a blueberry and growing fast. Hands and feet are forming from tiny paddle-shaped buds. The brain is producing about 100 new cells every minute. The digestive tract and lungs are starting to take shape. The face continues to develop with nostrils and a tiny mouth forming.
weeks.momBody: Your blood volume is increasing significantly. You might notice your waistline thickening slightly. Food aversions can be strong. Saliva production often increases (called ptyalism), which can worsen nausea. You may need to urinate very frequently.
tipsForWeek: Keep a food diary to identify safe foods versus trigger foods
Sip cold water through a straw if nausea makes drinking difficult
Wear loose, comfortable clothing as your waist expands
Don't be hard on yourself if your diet isn't perfect right now
weeks.nutritionTip: If you can only tolerate bland foods right now, that's okay. Focus on getting nutrients where you can — crackers, toast, rice, bananas, and applesauce are all fine.
weeks.exerciseTip: Swimming can be incredibly soothing if nausea is bad. The buoyancy relieves pressure and the cool water can ease discomfort.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby has all essential organs in their beginning stages. Tiny fingers and toes are forming (though they're still webbed). The baby is now making spontaneous movements, though you won't feel them yet. The tail that was visible in earlier weeks is disappearing. Eyes are developing pigment.
weeks.momBody: Your first prenatal appointment is likely around now. You may hear the heartbeat for the first time via doppler or see it on ultrasound — an emotional milestone! Breasts continue to grow and may feel heavy. You might notice visible blue veins on your breasts.
tipsForWeek: Prepare questions for your first prenatal appointment
Get a good supportive bra to ease breast discomfort
Start researching prenatal care options — OB vs midwife
Connect with other pregnant parents through apps or community groups
symptoms: Mild spotting after sex (usually normal — ask your doctor)
weeks.nutritionTip: Omega-3 fatty acids (DHA) support your baby's brain development. Sources include salmon, sardines, walnuts, chia seeds, and flaxseed. Many prenatal vitamins also include DHA.
weeks.exerciseTip: Kegel exercises are beneficial to start now. They strengthen the pelvic floor muscles that support your growing uterus and help with postpartum recovery.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby's fingers and toes are now more distinct, and the webbing is disappearing. Tiny earlobes are visible. The embryo is officially becoming a fetus this week — a major milestone! All major organs are present, though they'll continue to mature. The baby can now make tiny movements.
weeks.momBody: Your uterus is now about the size of a grapefruit. You may feel 'growing pains' as your ligaments stretch. Heartburn and indigestion may start. Some women begin to show a tiny belly bump. The first trimester tiredness may feel relentless — honor it.
tipsForWeek: Discuss genetic screening tests with your provider
Eat slowly and avoid lying down immediately after meals to reduce heartburn
Use a pillow between your knees for more comfortable sleep
Share your news with close family and friends if you feel ready
weeks.nutritionTip: Zinc supports cell growth and immune function. Good sources include meat, shellfish, legumes, seeds, and whole grains. Your prenatal vitamin should also contain zinc.
weeks.exerciseTip: Prenatal pilates is wonderful for building core strength gently. A strong core supports your growing belly and reduces back pain later in pregnancy.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is now officially a fetus! Tiny fingernails and toenails are beginning to form. The skeleton is changing from cartilage to bone. The brain is growing rapidly. Your baby can now open and close their tiny fists and swallow amniotic fluid. External genitalia are beginning to differentiate, though too early to tell on ultrasound.
weeks.momBody: You may finally start to feel a little more human soon — for many women, nausea begins to ease after week 10. Your clothing may feel tighter around the waist. Some women experience round ligament pain — sharp twinges in the lower abdomen when moving quickly.
tipsForWeek: NIPT (non-invasive prenatal testing) can be done from week 10 — discuss with your doctor
Consider investing in maternity clothing or belly bands
If nausea is severe (hyperemesis), contact your doctor about medication options
Start thinking about birth preferences and birth education classes
weeks.nutritionTip: Magnesium helps prevent leg cramps (common in pregnancy) and supports bone development. Find it in dark chocolate, avocado, nuts, seeds, and whole grains.
weeks.exerciseTip: Low-impact cardio like brisk walking, swimming, or stationary cycling is ideal. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is now about 4cm long and looks unmistakably human. Their head is still large relative to their body, but everything is proportioning out. The baby is moving around a lot in the amniotic sac, though you likely won't feel it. Hair follicles are forming. The liver is producing bile and the kidneys are producing urine.
weeks.momBody: The placenta is now taking over hormone production from the corpus luteum — this transition sometimes brings a brief easing of symptoms. Your uterus has moved up and out of your pelvis. Some women start to show noticeably now, especially if it's not their first pregnancy.
tipsForWeek: Book your nuchal translucency scan (usually done between weeks 11–14)
Start moisturizing your belly to help prevent stretch marks
Consider your dental health — pregnancy can affect gum health
Plan a comfortable sleep setup with extra pillows
symptoms: Slight relief from nausea for some
weeks.nutritionTip: Vitamin C helps with iron absorption and supports your immune system. Oranges, strawberries, bell peppers, and kiwi are excellent sources. Pair vitamin C with iron-rich foods for maximum benefit.
weeks.exerciseTip: Prenatal dance classes are a fun way to stay active and meet other expectant parents. Movement that brings you joy is always the best movement.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby's reflexes are developing — fingers open and close, toes curl, and eye muscles clench. The digestive system is beginning to practice contracting. The bone marrow is making white blood cells. Your baby has developed unique fingerprints! The face looks more human with eyes moving to the front of the face.
weeks.momBody: You've almost made it through the first trimester — congratulations! Risk of miscarriage drops significantly after week 12. Many women begin to feel more energetic. The uterus is now visible just above the pubic bone. Morning sickness often starts to improve for many women.
tipsForWeek: Many couples share their pregnancy news at 12 weeks — it's your choice when is right
Schedule your first trimester screening if not already done
Start exploring prenatal education classes
Begin thinking about your birth plan and support team
weeks.nutritionTip: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and reduces leg cramps. Bananas, sweet potatoes, avocado, and white beans are all excellent sources. Stay well hydrated too.
weeks.exerciseTip: As energy returns, you can gradually increase activity. Aim for a mix of cardio, strength, and flexibility work — all modified for pregnancy.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Welcome to the second trimester! Your baby is developing unique fingerprints and their vocal cords are forming. The intestines are moving from the umbilical cord into the abdomen. The pancreas is producing insulin. Your baby can now suck their thumb! Facial expressions are becoming possible.
weeks.momBody: The second trimester is often called the 'golden trimester' — most women experience a burst of energy and a decrease in nausea. Your belly is becoming more visible. Skin may start to glow with increased blood flow. Round ligament pain may continue as your uterus grows.
tipsForWeek: Celebrate making it to the second trimester!
Start sleeping on your left side to optimize blood flow to baby
Consider a pregnancy pillow for better sleep support
Begin researching childcare options if needed
weeks.nutritionTip: Your calorie needs increase by about 300–350 calories per day in the second trimester. Focus on nutrient-dense additions: nuts, avocado, whole grains, lean proteins.
weeks.exerciseTip: The second trimester is often the most comfortable for exercise. Consider joining a prenatal fitness class to connect with other mamas.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is sprouting fine hair called lanugo over their body — this helps regulate their temperature in the womb. The roof of the mouth is forming, and taste buds are developing. The baby is practicing breathing movements with amniotic fluid. Their legs are now longer than their arms.
weeks.momBody: Your energy levels are likely much improved. Your baby bump is becoming quite apparent. You may notice your hair looks thicker and shinier — due to pregnancy hormones slowing the normal hair shedding cycle. Skin changes like the linea nigra (a dark line on the belly) may appear.
tipsForWeek: Schedule your anatomy scan for around weeks 18–20
Look into maternity leave policies at your workplace
Start or continue Kegel exercises daily
Consider a prenatal massage for relaxation
weeks.nutritionTip: Choline is essential for your baby's brain and spinal cord development. Eggs are one of the best sources. Also found in beef liver, soybeans, chicken, and fish.
weeks.exerciseTip: Strength training with light weights is safe and beneficial during pregnancy. Focus on functional movements that support your changing body.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby can now sense light — if you shine a flashlight at your belly, they may move away from it! Bones are hardening further. The baby is making sucking and swallowing motions. Eyebrows and eyelashes are growing. The inner ear bones are hardening, which means your baby may be able to hear muffled sounds from outside the womb.
weeks.momBody: Some women begin to feel the first flutters of baby movement (called quickening) — it often feels like bubbles or butterflies. Your uterus is now about the size of a cantaloupe. Nosebleeds and bleeding gums are common due to increased blood volume. Skin may feel itchy as it stretches.
tipsForWeek: Talk, read, and sing to your baby — they may be starting to hear you!
Use a fragrance-free moisturizer on your growing belly to soothe itchy skin
If you haven't had an amniocentesis discussion, talk to your provider now if interested
Begin planning your nursery and baby essentials
weeks.nutritionTip: Iodine is critical for thyroid function and your baby's brain development. Sources include dairy products, eggs, seafood, and iodized salt. Many prenatal vitamins contain iodine.
weeks.exerciseTip: As your belly grows, modify exercises to avoid lying flat on your back for extended periods. Side-lying or propped positions are better for blood flow.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby's eyes are beginning to move slowly beneath closed eyelids — practicing the movements they'll need after birth. The baby can make facial expressions including squinting and frowning. Coordinated limb movements are happening. The circulatory system and urinary tract are fully functioning. Your baby's heart pumps about 25 quarts of blood per day.
weeks.momBody: You may feel your baby's movements more regularly now — especially if this is your second pregnancy. Your blood pressure may be lower than usual, which can cause dizziness if you stand up quickly. The 'pregnancy glow' is often most noticeable now with increased blood volume and oil production.
tipsForWeek: Start a kick count journal even though movements are irregular at this stage
Rise slowly from sitting or lying positions to prevent dizziness
Book your mid-pregnancy anatomy scan if not already scheduled
Consider whether you want to know the baby's sex
weeks.nutritionTip: Vitamin D supports bone development and immune function for both you and baby. Sunlight is the best source, but fatty fish, egg yolks, and fortified foods also help. Consider supplementation if levels are low.
weeks.exerciseTip: Water aerobics is fantastic in the second trimester — the water supports your weight and keeps you cool while providing resistance.

weeks.babyDevelopment: A layer of fat is beginning to form under your baby's skin — this will be crucial for regulating body temperature after birth. The baby's skeleton is changing from soft cartilage to hardening bone. Sweat glands are developing. Your baby's sense of hearing is increasingly sharp — they can hear your heartbeat, your voice, and even music.
weeks.momBody: Your uterus now sits about 5cm below your belly button. Some women experience a heightened sense of smell or unusual food cravings. Varicose veins may start to appear as blood volume increases. The growing uterus can cause sciatic nerve pain — sharp pain radiating down the back and leg.
tipsForWeek: Wear compression socks to prevent varicose veins and leg swelling
If sciatica starts, a physio or chiropractor can help
Play music to your belly — your baby loves it!
Start researching childbirth education classes in your area
weeks.nutritionTip: Fiber is your best friend for preventing constipation, which is common in pregnancy. Aim for 25–30g daily from fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes.
weeks.exerciseTip: Pelvic tilts and cat-cow stretches relieve back pain and keep your spine flexible. Do them throughout the day, not just during dedicated exercise sessions.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is now yawning, hiccuping, rolling, twisting, and making faces. The bones of the inner ear are now hard, giving your baby full hearing capability. They can hear your voice clearly — you are their favorite sound in the world! Myelin (a protective sheath) is beginning to form around the nerves.
weeks.momBody: Your belly button may begin to pop outward as your uterus pushes against it. You may feel your baby's hiccups — a rhythmic pulsing sensation. Back pain, leg cramps, and swollen feet may increase. Sleep is becoming more challenging as the bump grows.
tipsForWeek: Your anatomy scan is coming up around weeks 18–20 — an exciting milestone!
Elevate your feet when sitting to reduce ankle swelling
Start sleeping with a pregnancy pillow between your knees
Write letters or voice messages to your baby — a beautiful keepsake
weeks.nutritionTip: Probiotics support digestive health, which can help with constipation and support your immune system. Yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, and kimchi are good sources.
weeks.exerciseTip: Side-lying exercises are comfortable at this stage. Practice side-lying leg lifts and clamshells to strengthen your hips and reduce pelvic discomfort.

weeks.babyDevelopment: A white, creamy coating called vernix caseosa is now covering your baby's skin to protect it from the amniotic fluid. The sensory brain areas that process smell, taste, sight, sound, and touch are developing. If you're having a girl, she already has about 6 million eggs in her ovaries! Your baby is becoming more and more responsive.
weeks.momBody: You are likely feeling baby kicks regularly now — these are definitive movements, not just flutters. Your uterus reaches your belly button this week. Appetite may be very strong. Some women experience a metallic taste in their mouth or unusual cravings (sometimes for non-food items — tell your doctor if this happens).
tipsForWeek: Begin formally tracking fetal movements (kick counts) daily
Discuss your anatomy scan results with your provider thoroughly
Register for a childbirth class if you haven't yet
If you have a feeling about baby's sex, now is often when you find out!
weeks.nutritionTip: Your iron needs are increasing significantly. Red meat, poultry, beans, lentils, tofu, and fortified cereals all provide iron. Always take iron with vitamin C to boost absorption.
weeks.exerciseTip: Balance and stability become increasingly important as your center of gravity shifts. Try standing on one leg (near a wall for safety), or gentle balance ball exercises.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Halfway there — congratulations! Your baby is now about 16cm from head to bottom. They can hear music and voices clearly. Sleep and wake cycles are becoming established. Fingernails are growing to the tips of the fingers. Your baby may even startle at loud noises. They're getting quite active in there!
weeks.momBody: This is the halfway milestone — you're doing amazingly! The anatomy scan around this time is a big highlight. Your uterus is now at your belly button. Braxton Hicks contractions (practice contractions that are painless and irregular) may begin. Skin changes like chloasma (skin darkening on the face) may appear.
tipsForWeek: Celebrate the halfway point — you've done an incredible job!
Take a 20-week bump photo — you'll treasure it forever
Review your anatomy scan results and ask about placenta position
Think about your birth preferences and discuss with your provider
weeks.nutritionTip: Your blood volume has increased by nearly 50%. Make sure you're getting enough iron and staying well hydrated to support this incredible cardiovascular demand.
weeks.exerciseTip: Congratulate yourself! Stay active with activities you enjoy. Many women continue running, cycling, and lifting weights well into the second trimester with modifications.

weeks.babyDevelopment: From this point, babies are measured from head to toe rather than head to bottom. Your baby weighs about 360g. The digestive system is active — the baby swallows amniotic fluid and absorbs sugars and nutrients from it. Eyebrows and eyelids are now fully formed. The baby is beginning to look more like a newborn every day.
weeks.momBody: Your belly is very visible now. Linea nigra (the dark line down your abdomen) is usually present. You may experience a 'pregnancy nose' — swelling of nasal tissues due to increased blood flow. Carpal tunnel syndrome (tingling and numbness in hands and wrists) can develop. Stretch marks may become more visible.
tipsForWeek: Use a belly band for extra support during physical activity
Carpal tunnel wrist splints can help with hand tingling
Make sure your car seat belt fits safely under your bump
Start or deepen your connection with your baby through talking and music
weeks.nutritionTip: Collagen and protein support skin elasticity, which may help with stretch marks. Include enough lean protein, and consider bone broth or collagen-rich foods. Hydration is equally important.
weeks.exerciseTip: Prenatal yoga is particularly beneficial now for hip opening, back relief, and breathing practice. Many of the poses you learn will be useful during labor.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby's senses are developing rapidly — they can now perceive light, dark, and color differences through the uterine wall. The inner ear is fully formed and the baby can balance in the fluid. Lips are becoming more distinct. The pancreas is producing the hormones insulin and glucagon to regulate blood sugar.
weeks.momBody: Your fundal height (the distance from pubic bone to top of uterus) is roughly equal to your weeks of pregnancy now. You may experience symphysis pubis dysfunction — pain in the front of the pelvis. Your center of gravity is shifting, changing how you walk and balance.
tipsForWeek: A physiotherapist can help with pelvic girdle pain — don't just push through it
Practice good posture to minimize back and hip pain
Consider hypnobirthing or other birth preparation methods
Check in on your mental health — prenatal anxiety is common and treatable
weeks.nutritionTip: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health. Green leafy vegetables, broccoli, and fermented foods are rich sources. It's also important for your newborn after birth.
weeks.exerciseTip: Hip circles on a birth ball are wonderful for pelvic floor release and relieving pelvic pressure. Many hospitals also use birth balls during labor.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby now weighs just over 500g — a big milestone! At this stage, babies born prematurely have some chance of survival with intensive neonatal care. The lungs are developing rapidly, though not yet ready for air breathing. Your baby is developing a regular sleep-wake pattern, and you may notice more activity at certain times of day.
weeks.momBody: Braxton Hicks contractions may be more noticeable now. Your belly button may be fully popped. Sleeping is becoming increasingly difficult — pillows are your best friend. You may notice your feet getting a half size or full size larger due to relaxin hormone loosening ligaments.
tipsForWeek: Learn the signs of preterm labor and when to call your provider
Invest in comfortable, supportive footwear — your feet may have grown
Practice relaxation techniques for better sleep
Talk to your employer about your maternity leave plan
weeks.nutritionTip: Your baby's lung development depends on adequate protein, antioxidants (vitamins C and E), and omega-3s. Varied, colorful eating covers most bases. Keep up the good work!
weeks.exerciseTip: If Braxton Hicks become frequent during exercise, slow down and hydrate. They're usually triggered by exertion or dehydration and resolve with rest and fluids.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby reaches the 'viability milestone' — at 24 weeks, babies can survive outside the womb with intensive medical support. The lungs are producing surfactant — a substance that will help the air sacs inflate after birth. The brain is developing billions of neurons. Your baby's face is almost fully formed.
weeks.momBody: Your uterus is now about the size of a soccer ball. You'll have the glucose challenge test (gestational diabetes screening) around now. Heartburn is often more intense as the uterus pushes against the stomach. You may feel your ribs being kicked for the first time!
tipsForWeek: Get your gestational diabetes screening (glucose challenge test)
Eat smaller, more frequent meals to manage heartburn
Prop yourself up with pillows to sleep — it helps with reflux
Tour the hospital or birth center where you plan to deliver
weeks.nutritionTip: If you're diagnosed with gestational diabetes, work with a dietitian to create a meal plan. Focus on low-glycemic carbohydrates, plenty of fiber, protein, and healthy fats.
weeks.exerciseTip: Regular exercise helps prevent and manage gestational diabetes. Walking after meals is particularly effective for blood sugar control.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is gaining weight rapidly — about 6 ounces per week. The capillaries forming under the skin are filling with blood, giving the skin a pink tinge. The hands are fully developed and the baby practices grasping. The spine is getting stronger. Your baby now responds to your touch — if you press on your belly, they may push back!
weeks.momBody: Your bump is now very prominent. The top of your uterus sits between your belly button and ribcage. Shortness of breath is common as the uterus pushes against the diaphragm. Hemorrhoids may worsen. You may notice your rings getting tight due to fluid retention.
tipsForWeek: Remove rings before they get too tight due to swelling
Sleep elevated to help with shortness of breath and reflux
Start choosing a pediatrician or family doctor for baby
Practice perineal massage to prepare for labor
weeks.nutritionTip: Your baby's bone density is increasing rapidly now. Ensure you're getting 1000mg calcium daily from dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, almonds, and white beans.
weeks.exerciseTip: Resistance band exercises are gentle but effective for maintaining strength. They're easy to use at home and can be modified as your pregnancy progresses.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby's eyes are opening for the first time! Though vision is limited to light and dark, this is a remarkable developmental milestone. The immune system is maturing. Your baby can hear familiar voices clearly — studies show newborns recognize their mother's voice immediately after birth. Brain wave activity is beginning to show REM (dream) sleep patterns.
weeks.momBody: You may feel significant fetal activity now — kicks, rolls, and stretches are all common. Your body is producing more of the hormone relaxin, which loosens ligaments throughout your body. This prepares the pelvis for birth but can cause joint pain and instability.
tipsForWeek: Establish a daily kick count routine — aim to feel 10 movements in 2 hours
Consider a pregnancy support belt for back and round ligament relief
Read or play music to your belly — your baby is truly listening
Start gathering newborn essentials if you haven't already
weeks.nutritionTip: B vitamins (especially B12, B6, and folate) support your nervous system and baby's brain development. Animal products, fortified cereals, leafy greens, and legumes are key sources.
weeks.exerciseTip: Birthing ball exercises like gentle bouncing and pelvic circles help position the baby optimally and relieve pelvic pressure. Use one at your desk instead of a chair!

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby now weighs about 875g and can open and close their eyes at will. Taste buds are fully developed and your baby can taste the flavors of what you eat through the amniotic fluid. Brain tissue is increasing significantly. The lungs, while still maturing, are capable of breathing air with medical support if born now.
weeks.momBody: The third trimester is just around the corner. Fatigue is often returning. Your uterus now reaches 3–4 inches above your belly button. Leg cramps are very common. You may experience Restless Leg Syndrome at night — an irresistible urge to move the legs. Colostrum leakage from the breasts may increase.
tipsForWeek: Welcome to the home stretch — the third trimester begins next week!
Discuss your birth plan with your provider
Stretch your calves before bed to prevent leg cramps
For restless legs, try warm baths, stretching, and reducing caffeine
weeks.nutritionTip: Eating foods rich in flavors you want your child to enjoy — research shows babies develop taste preferences in the womb based on what you eat. It's a great time to eat those vegetables!
weeks.exerciseTip: Gentle evening stretches, especially calf stretches, can prevent the leg cramps that disturb sleep. A short walk after dinner also helps circulation.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Welcome to the third trimester! Your baby weighs about 1kg and measures around 37cm. The brain is developing more complex folding and creasing. Eyelashes are now fully formed. The baby's position is increasingly important — most babies turn head-down (vertex position) in the coming weeks. Fat continues to be deposited under the skin.
weeks.momBody: Your healthcare provider will likely schedule more frequent appointments. You may have your Rh factor testing and get an anti-D injection if needed. Sleep is often very disrupted now. The belly may feel very large and tight. Swollen feet and ankles are common by end of day.
tipsForWeek: Start your birth plan document
Attend or plan your hospital tour
Pack your hospital bag checklist now — even if birth is weeks away
Discuss any birth fears or concerns openly with your provider
weeks.nutritionTip: Third trimester calorie needs increase by about 450 calories. Focus on quality: complex carbs, healthy fats, lean protein. Iron is especially critical as you build stores for postpartum recovery.
weeks.exerciseTip: Walking is the single best exercise for the third trimester. It encourages baby into optimal position, keeps you fit, and is easy to do daily.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby's muscles and lungs are continuing to mature rapidly. The brain is growing very quickly, with billions of neurons making connections. Your baby weighs about 1.15kg. The skeleton is fully formed but still soft and flexible for the birth journey. The baby's movements may feel different as space becomes more limited — rolling instead of kicking.
weeks.momBody: You may notice the baby's movements have changed character — less wild kicks and more rolling, stretching, and hiccupping. Swelling is often more pronounced, especially in the evening. You may feel pressure on your bladder almost constantly. Hemorrhoids may worsen.
tipsForWeek: Do kick counts at the same time every day for consistency
Elevate your feet whenever sitting to reduce swelling
Stay off your back when sleeping — left side is best
Start or finalize your maternity leave paperwork
weeks.nutritionTip: Constipation is very common in the third trimester. Prunes, kiwi fruit, flaxseed, and plenty of water are your best allies. Move your body daily to help too.
weeks.exerciseTip: Swimming is especially wonderful in the third trimester because the water supports your full weight, relieving joints and back. Even floating is beneficial!

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 1.3kg. The bone marrow is now making all red blood cells (previously the liver handled this). The wrinkled skin is beginning to smooth as fat fills in underneath. Your baby can track light with their eyes. The brain and nervous system are sophisticated enough to control body temperature.
weeks.momBody: You have 10 weeks to go — you're in the final stretch! Shortness of breath is very common as the uterus pushes against the diaphragm. The linea nigra is dark and prominent. Braxton Hicks may be becoming more frequent. Your navel may be very stretched or inverted.
tipsForWeek: Ten weeks to go — take a proud bump photo!
Enroll in newborn care or breastfeeding classes
Discuss pain management options for labor with your provider
Prepare your postpartum support plan — who will help you?
weeks.nutritionTip: Your baby is absorbing significant calcium from your bones. Make sure your intake is adequate — 1000–1300mg/day. Deficiency can increase your risk of osteoporosis later.
weeks.exerciseTip: Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) are more important than ever now. Do sets of 10 contractions several times a day to prepare for labor and postpartum recovery.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 1.5kg and all five senses are functioning. The brain is maturing rapidly and forming trillions of synaptic connections. Your baby is moving into a more cramped position as they grow. Lanugo (fine body hair) is starting to disappear from the face. The irises of the eyes can now dilate and contract in response to light.
weeks.momBody: You may feel your baby's hiccups daily. Leaky breasts (colostrum) are common and completely normal. You may start to feel very full very quickly when eating — the uterus is compressing the stomach. Nesting instinct may kick in with a strong urge to clean and prepare.
tipsForWeek: Embrace the nesting instinct — but don't overdo it
Stock your freezer with easy postpartum meals
Research breastfeeding support resources in your area
Pre-register at the hospital to speed up admission when the time comes
weeks.nutritionTip: Small, frequent meals are the key to managing third trimester discomfort. Six small meals instead of three large ones is much easier on your compressed digestive system.
weeks.exerciseTip: Slow walks, gentle yoga, and birthing ball exercises are all ideal in late pregnancy. Honor your body's limits — you're doing an incredible amount of work just existing right now.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 1.7kg. The lungs are well developed and practice breathing movements are happening frequently. Toenails are fully grown. The baby is gaining about half a pound per week now. If you're having a boy, the testicles have moved from the abdomen to the scrotum. Most babies are settling into a head-down position.
weeks.momBody: You may have more frequent prenatal appointments now (every 2 weeks). Movement has likely shifted from wild kicks to rolls, wiggles, and stretches. Some women feel a strong emotional pull toward their baby and partner during this time. Sleep deprivation may be significant.
tipsForWeek: Confirm your baby's position at your next appointment
If baby is breech, discuss options with your provider — there's still time to turn
Finalize your hospital bag packing
Have a frank conversation about your support network for early postpartum
weeks.nutritionTip: Your baby is storing iron at a rapid rate now. Keep up iron-rich eating and absorption-boosting vitamin C. This is also when your baby stores most of their brown fat for warmth after birth.
weeks.exerciseTip: Forward-leaning positions (all fours, leaning over a birth ball) encourage optimal fetal positioning — getting baby head-down and facing your spine (occiput anterior).

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 1.9kg — nearly 2kg! The bones are hardening except for the skull, which remains soft and flexible to allow passage through the birth canal. The immune system is boosted through antibodies passed from you via the placenta. Your baby's coordination is improving — they can grasp their own foot!
weeks.momBody: Pelvic pressure may intensify as the baby's head engages (drops lower into the pelvis) — this is called 'lightening.' Breathing becomes easier once lightening happens, but bladder pressure increases. You may feel very clumsy and unbalanced. False labor (Braxton Hicks) may be more intense.
tipsForWeek: Know the difference between Braxton Hicks and true labor contractions
Create your birth support playlist
Prep a postpartum recovery kit for yourself
Write down your newborn care questions for the pediatrician
weeks.nutritionTip: In the final weeks, your body is transferring critical stores of vitamins (A, D, B12) and minerals (calcium, iron, zinc) to your baby. Don't let nutrition slip now — this is the final push!
weeks.exerciseTip: Continue gentle activity but listen to your body completely. On days when pelvic pressure is intense, rest. On better days, walk, swim, or do gentle yoga.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby now weighs about 2.1kg. The vernix caseosa (waxy coating) is thickening. Their central nervous system and lungs are well-matured. Babies born at 34 weeks have excellent outcomes with minimal intervention. All organs are functioning. The fat deposits are filling out the face, making it look round and babylike.
weeks.momBody: You may feel very large and uncomfortable now. The baby's head may be pressing on your sciatic nerve. Swollen ankles may be very pronounced by evening. Watch for signs of preeclampsia: sudden severe swelling, headache, visual changes — call your doctor immediately if these occur.
tipsForWeek: Know the warning signs of preeclampsia and call immediately if they appear
Monitor your blood pressure if you have a home cuff
Prepare your 'go bag' and put it by the door
Have a clear plan for who to call when labor starts
weeks.nutritionTip: Hydration is especially important now for amniotic fluid levels and to prevent Braxton Hicks. Drink water consistently throughout the day, not just when thirsty.
weeks.exerciseTip: Rest is exercise now. Your body is doing an enormous amount of work. Gentle movement like slow walks is valuable, but rest without guilt when your body asks for it.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 2.4kg and is plumping up beautifully. The kidneys are fully developed. The liver can process some waste products. Most of the lanugo has disappeared. Your baby is getting ready — practicing sucking and swallowing, breathing, and regulating their own body temperature.
weeks.momBody: You may be getting tested for Group B Strep (GBS) around now — a routine swab that determines if you need antibiotics in labor. Lightening may have occurred, making your belly appear lower. Sleep is very difficult. Many women feel a strange mix of 'can't wait to meet baby' and 'I'm not ready!'
tipsForWeek: Group B Strep test usually happens this week — it's quick and painless
Finalize your birth plan and give copies to your support people
Install the infant car seat and have it inspected
Pre-wash all baby clothes and bedding in gentle detergent
weeks.nutritionTip: Raspberry leaf tea is traditionally used to tone the uterus in late pregnancy — discuss with your midwife before starting. Some providers recommend it from 36 weeks onward.
weeks.exerciseTip: Dates are rich in nutrients and some research suggests eating 6 dates daily from 36 weeks may support cervical ripening. Talk to your provider about this! Meanwhile, keep moving gently.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 2.6kg and is considered 'early term' from this week. The skull plates are designed to overlap slightly to navigate the birth canal. Cheeks are chubby from fat deposits. The immune system is continuing to develop. Your baby is likely in final birth position — head down, facing your spine.
weeks.momBody: Your provider will now check for cervical changes — dilation and effacement. You may lose the mucus plug (a thick discharge) as the cervix begins to soften. Braxton Hicks may be stronger and more frequent. Any contraction pattern that becomes regular should be evaluated.
tipsForWeek: Learn to time contractions accurately
Know your hospital's protocol — when to call, when to go in
Rest and savor these last weeks — they pass so quickly
Write a letter to your baby about your hopes and dreams for them
weeks.nutritionTip: Start eating 6 Medjool dates per day if your provider approves. Research shows they may help ripen the cervix and reduce the need for labor induction. They're also a great energy source!
weeks.exerciseTip: Curb walking (walking with one foot on the curb, one on the road) and stair climbing can help encourage baby's descent. These old wives' tale exercises actually have some merit!

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is considered 'full term' this week! They weigh about 2.9kg. The brain and lungs, though fully functional, continue to mature — every extra day in the womb counts. Your baby has a firm grasp and can recognize familiar voices. Fat deposits are nearly complete, giving them that adorable newborn roundness.
weeks.momBody: You may feel very 'done' with pregnancy at this point — and that's completely normal. The weight of the baby plus amniotic fluid and placenta is significant. Your whole body is working overtime. Pre-labor signs like increased Braxton Hicks, diarrhea, and increased discharge are common.
tipsForWeek: Baby is full term — celebrate this milestone!
Trust your instincts — you know your body and baby
Rest, hydrate, and nourish yourself for the marathon ahead
Do something special for yourself — a massage, a bath, a date with your partner
weeks.nutritionTip: Eat well-balanced meals to build energy reserves for labor. Labor is physically demanding — think of these last weeks as fueling your muscles and glycogen stores for the big event.
weeks.exerciseTip: Daily walks, birthing ball exercises, and pelvic tilts all help prepare your body and baby for birth. Even 20 minutes a day makes a meaningful difference.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 3.1kg and is putting on roughly 30g per day. The brain and nervous system continue to mature. The placenta is still providing nutrients and antibodies. Your baby's intestines are accumulating meconium — a dark, sticky substance that will be their first bowel movement. Fingernails may already extend beyond the fingertips.
weeks.momBody: Some women experience prodromal (early) labor — regular contractions that don't progress to active labor. This can be exhausting and confusing. True labor contractions become longer, stronger, and closer together over time. Your provider may do cervical checks at appointments.
tipsForWeek: Learn to distinguish prodromal labor from true labor
Rest as much as possible — labor may be soon
Review your birth plan one final time with your support team
Make sure someone is designated to care for pets and older children during labor
weeks.nutritionTip: Keep snacks handy for early labor — you'll need energy! Light, easily digestible foods like dates, toast with peanut butter, yogurt, and fruit are ideal.
weeks.exerciseTip: Acupressure points for labor stimulation (hands, feet, ankles) can be explored with a trained practitioner. Spicy foods and sex — also rumored triggers — though evidence is limited, both are harmless if desired!

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby weighs about 3.3kg — a full, beautiful, healthy baby ready to meet you! The brain and lungs continue to mature right up to birth. The skull bones are still loose to navigate the birth canal. Your baby's nails may need trimming shortly after birth. Their skin is smooth and their body is fully plump and ready for the world.
weeks.momBody: You could go into labor any day now! Signs of labor to watch for: regular contractions every 5 minutes lasting 60 seconds, water breaking, bloody show, or a strong 'something's different' feeling. Trust your body — it knows what to do.
tipsForWeek: Stay calm and trust your body — billions of women have done this before you
Keep your phone charged and your hospital bag at the door
Sleep, rest, and eat well while you can
Express gratitude for this incredible journey — you are amazing
weeks.nutritionTip: Eat light meals during early labor to maintain energy without overloading your digestive system. Many hospitals allow light eating in early labor now. Stay well hydrated.
weeks.exerciseTip: Slow dancing with your partner during labor can help baby descend. Walking, swaying, and changing positions frequently are all helpful for labor progress.

weeks.babyDevelopment: Your baby is fully ready for the world — typically weighing between 3–4kg and measuring about 50–52cm. Their immune system carries antibodies from you to protect them in early life. Their brain will continue developing for years after birth. Their lungs are fully prepared to take their first breath. Everything is ready — it's almost time!
weeks.momBody: Due dates are estimates — only 5% of babies arrive exactly on their due date. If you've reached 40 weeks, your provider will discuss monitoring and possibly induction options if you go significantly past due. Trust your body, trust your baby, and know that you are ready for this incredible moment.
tipsForWeek: Your due date is here — baby will arrive in their own perfect time
Stay in close contact with your healthcare provider after 40 weeks
Rest, stay hydrated, and eat nourishing food
You are strong, prepared, and ready. You've got this, mama!
weeks.nutritionTip: You've nourished a complete human being for 40 weeks — that is an extraordinary achievement. After birth, continue nourishing yourself to support recovery and breastfeeding if you choose.
weeks.exerciseTip: You've made it! Labor itself is the final workout — your body has been preparing for this for 40 weeks. Trust the process, breathe through contractions, and know that you are capable of this. You are strong and ready.
